newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebel leader in Kisangani for refugee talks.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebel leader in Kisangani for refugee talks.

text.p: Rebel leader Laurent Kabila arrived in northeastern Zaire on Saturday for talks on a refugee crisis involving 100,000 Rwandans which he says is being unfairly blamed on his troops.
Kabila flew to the city of Kisangani from Lubumbashi and went straight into talks with his aides, diplomats and aid agency representatives.
"He is holding consultations with various people. These include his aides, diplomats and aid agency officials," a rebel official told Reuters.

Kabila and officials of his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) say the crisis had been blown out of proportion and refuse to accept blanket responsibility for the fate of the refugees.
Many come from a hardcore militia accused of taking part in Rwanda's 1994 genocide of Tutsis and moderate Hutus and refuse to return home for fear of reprisals.
Kabila told Reuters earlier that criminals among the refugees had transported their lawlessness to Zaire where the Alliance is waging a war against their allies.
"Many among the refugees are criminals who are attacking local Zaireans and engaging in acts of criminality," Kabila said.
International outrage over the refugees, who scattered this week from three sites south of Kisangani, has tunred into a major public relations disaster for Kabila's seven-month rebellion.

U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan described rebel treatment of the refugees as "slow extermination" and a U.N. food agency spokeswoman, making a comparison with Hitler's Germany, said: "The expression 'Final Solution' is not exaggerated."
Paul Stromberg, of the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR, said: "The visit of Kabila will provide us with the opportunity to take up his offer of access to U.N. agencies and to seek an overall solution."
Stromberg said Kabila was expected to meet Aldo Aiello, the European Union special envoy to the Great Lakes region, and Pierce Gerety, U.N. humanitarian coordinator for the region.

He said aid agencies would send teams to wherever Kabila's forces allowed access but added that the rebels had decided that security from km seven (mile four) to km 82 (mile 50) south of Kisangani was not good enough.
"We sent out a plane and it appears the refugee population previously at km 82 had left," he said.
"We put down in Ubundu (a town 100 km (60 miles) south of Kisangani) and saw a total of 117 refugees who said they came down from km 82 last night after being harassed by the local population."
Stromberg said there had been 2,500 refugees at km 82 before aid agencies were blocked this week from reaching the refugees south of Kisangani.
"We can see from the air the plastic sheeting has gone so it appears that all the refugees there have left," he said.

About 85,000 refugees abandoned two camps south of Kisangani this week after fighting there and disappeared into the jungle, where aid workers fear that thousands who were already malnourished and sick will soon perish without aid.

Kabila, whose rebels have seized more than half of Zaire since October, has forecast a swift battle for Kinshasa, the capital, as a rift developed over venues for any talks with ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko.
In Luanda, the Angolan government denied charges by authorities in Kinshasa that Angolan troops had crossed into Zaire from the northern enclave of Cabinda to help the rebels.
